title: The wild elephant
hook: Devadatta sets the elephant Nalagiri loose; the Buddha meets it with metta and it kneels (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Patacara, who lost everyone and heard: sister, recover your mind. Your line: recover your mind.

Someone you trusted turns on you. Not a stranger. Family. That has its own particular sting. Devadatta was the Buddha's cousin, and a monk in his own order. Over the years, the old texts say, he grew jealous, then ambitious. He asked to be put in charge of the whole community, and was refused. After that, he tried to kill the Buddha. Once he hired men to ambush him. Once he rolled a boulder down a hillside, and a splinter of rock cut the Buddha's foot. Then, in the city of Rajagaha, he went to the royal stables, where a huge, fierce elephant named Nalagiri was kept.
screen: `WHEN FAMILY TURNS ON YOU.` → `DEVADATTA, THE JEALOUS COUSIN.` → `A FIERCE ELEPHANT NAMED NALAGIRI.`

segments.voice: Devadatta tells the keepers: when the monk Gotama comes down this street on his alms round, let Nalagiri loose. Later tellings add that the keepers gave him strong drink first, to make him wilder. In the morning the Buddha walks into the street with his monks, and there's Nalagiri, trunk up, ears spread, tail stiff, charging. People scramble onto rooftops. The monks beg him to turn back. He tells them not to be afraid. Then he does the thing this whole path keeps returning to: he meets the elephant with metta, loving-kindness, spreading goodwill toward the animal charging him. Not a trick. Not a weapon. Just a mind with no hatred in it, pointed at a creature full of rage. Nalagiri lowers his trunk and slows. He comes up to the Buddha and stands still, and the Buddha strokes his forehead. The texts say the elephant took dust from the Buddha's feet onto his own head, and walked back to his stable, calm. In the paintings, he kneels. The Dhammapada has a line for this, in Max Müller's old translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." Look back at this week. A killer on the forest road, and a monk who walked on. I have stopped; you stop. Angulimala, stoned in town, and blessing a birth. Kisa Gotami, carrying her son everywhere, and no house untouched. Patacara: sister, recover your mind. And today, an elephant, kneeling. Each is about meeting the worst with something steadier than it.
screen: `LET THE ELEPHANT LOOSE.` · `MET WITH METTA.` · `DUST FROM HIS FEET.` · `A WEEK OF HARD STORIES.` · then, large: `THE ELEPHANT KNEELS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that reliably makes you angry, a certain tone or person, and feel the heat start, the trunk going up. Instead of charging back, breathe out slowly and send it goodwill, the way the Buddha did: may you be at ease; may you be free of this rage. Watch what happens to the heat.
Nalagiri. The wild elephant set loose by Devadatta and met with loving-kindness, who lowered his trunk and walked home calm.
Your line: the elephant kneels. A week of hard stories, one steady thread. See you on day seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhist art shows the taming of Nalagiri, often with the elephant kneeling, and metta, loving-kindness meditation, is practiced in Buddhist traditions as the quality the Buddha showed here.

what a scholar hears: Vinaya, Cullavagga 7.3; Nalagiri's taming is among the 'eight great events' shown in Pala-period art; the kneeling is the artists' picture, the text says he lowered his trunk.
